tagline: Gorilla forests on the great river's bank
overview:
The Republic of the Congo, often called Congo-Brazzaville to tell it apart from its much bigger neighbor, lies on the equator in Central Africa. It is a little smaller than Montana, with a short Atlantic coastline and long borders with Gabon, Cameroon, the Central African Republic, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The capital, Brazzaville, faces Kinshasa, capital of the DR Congo, directly across the Congo River, making them the two closest capital cities in the world after Rome and Vatican City.

Around 6 million people live here, and more than half of them are in Brazzaville or the port city of Pointe-Noire. French is the official language, and Lingala and Kikongo are widely spoken. Oil pumped from beneath the ocean provides most of the country's money, along with timber from its vast forests. The Republic of the Congo is a presidential republic, led for most of the time since 1979 by the same president. Rainforest covers about two-thirds of the land, sheltering some of the largest gorilla and elephant populations left in Africa.
landAndNature: A narrow coastal plain rises to the Mayombe hills, then dips into the fertile Niari valley before climbing to the Batéké Plateau, a high grassland of sandy soil and deep river gorges. North of it spreads the Congo Basin rainforest and one of the largest tropical swamp forests on Earth, where rivers wander through flooded woodland for hundreds of kilometers. Odzala-Kokoua National Park holds tens of thousands of western lowland gorillas along with forest elephants, chimpanzees, and bongo antelope, and Nouabalé-Ndoki park is so remote that its animals show little fear of humans. The Congo River, second only to the Amazon in water flow, forms much of the eastern border. Rain falls heavily most of the year, and the climate is hot and steamy.
peopleAndCulture: The Kongo people are the largest group, followed by the Teke, Mbochi, and Sangha, with forest peoples living in the north. Most Congolese are Christian. Cassava is the main food, eaten as chikwangue, a dense loaf wrapped in leaves, or as saka-saka, pounded cassava leaves cooked with palm oil and fish. Grilled fish and plantains are sold at roadside stands. Brazzaville shares with Kinshasa the birth of Congolese rumba, a swaying guitar music recognized by UNESCO, and its streets are famous for the sapeurs, men who dress in dazzling tailored suits and treat elegance as an art form. Soccer is the most popular sport, and the country's writers, such as Alain Mabanckou, have won major French literary prizes.
history: Bantu-speaking peoples settled the region long ago, and by the 1400s the Kingdom of Kongo and the Teke kingdom traded ivory and copper. Portuguese contact from 1482 led to centuries of slave trading from the coast. In 1880 the French-Italian explorer Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza signed a treaty with the Teke king, and France made the area a colony, later the capital of French Equatorial Africa; forced labor building a railway to the coast killed thousands. Brazzaville served as the capital of Free France during World War II. Independence came on August 15, 1960. A Marxist government ruled from 1969 to 1991. Denis Sassou Nguesso held power from 1979 to 1992, and after a civil war in 1997 he returned and has governed since.
funFacts: Brazzaville and Kinshasa are the only two national capitals in the world that face each other across a river.
The Congo River is so powerful that it pushes fresh water more than 100 kilometers out into the Atlantic Ocean.
Sapeurs of Brazzaville may save for months to buy a single designer suit, then parade it through the streets on weekends.
The country's swamp forests store enormous amounts of carbon in peat, in some places more than five meters deep.
During World War II, Brazzaville was for a time the capital of the Free French forces fighting Nazi Germany.
